Fitting random labels

Deep networks fit random labels, then perform at chance on test images. Zhang et al., 2016 ↗

GeneralizationOptimization

Claims

SupportsLimitsChallenges
V1Deep networks fit random labels without changing architecture or training hyperparameters 88406

Suggested status Ccontested

Several independent groups reproduce random-label fitting, with WideResNet-18 showing test performance near chance after fitting random labels. Keeping training hyperparameters unchanged is disputed: VGG-19 required a lower learning rate.

Original resultZhang et al., 2016 ↗

Zhang et al. trained networks on randomly labeled CIFAR10 and ImageNet under different regularization settings.

With weight decay on CIFAR10, Inception and MLP 3x512 reached 100% training accuracy, while Alexnet failed to converge. On ImageNet, Inception V3 reached 87.81–95.20% top-1 training accuracy across the reported regularization settings.

§4.1, Figure 5

Related findings6 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Interpolation constructions require explicit assumptions 25 studies

Networks can be constructed to fit arbitrary labels under specific constraints on their architecture, input geometry and parameters. These guarantees about capacity alone do not show that stochastic gradient training will converge.

  • Constructed two-layer ReLU networks fit arbitrary labels on inputs in general position, without establishing SGD convergence. Sébastien Bubeck et al., 2020 ↗
  • A width-2 network of specified depth fits any nonnegative class labels on distinct inputs. Martín Hernández et al., 2024 ↗
  • Required side-network size grows approximately with the square root of changed random targets. Jy-yong Sohn et al., 2024 ↗
Models and training procedures differ in fitting random labels 17 studies

Arbitrary-target fitting and its generalization cost depend on architecture, effective capacity, data and training procedure. Some tested models fit random labels completely, while others remain far from complete fitting.

  • Greedily spectrally trained KNet perfectly fits random labels, with the test chance level unspecified. Chieh-Tsai Wu et al., 2020 ↗
  • Spline-only KAN (Kolmogorov-Arnold network) fits random MNIST labels poorly across the reported training budgets. Yun-Hao Ni et al., 2026 ↗
  • Under partial label noise, the quantum head loses less peak-to-final test accuracy than the classical head. Yasoda Lasiru Ariyarathna Epa et al., 2026 ↗
Other model families also fit arbitrary labels 5 studies

Linear classifiers, kernels, Gaussian processes and random forests can fit randomized or partially corrupted targets under suitable capacity and data conditions. Their generalization depends on the model and setting.

  • Weakly regularized logistic regression memorizes randomized MNIST labels and makes random, overconfident test predictions. Samuel L. Smith et al., 2017 ↗
  • A Gaussian process with an RBF kernel perfectly fits random CIFAR-10 labels despite low test accuracy. A. Wilson et al., 2020 ↗
  • Maximum-margin linear classifiers have unseen-data error bounds under stated assumptions and fit noisy Boolean simulations exactly. Niladri S. Chatterji et al., 2020 ↗
Classifiers on fixed representations test a distinct fitting capacity 5 studies

Classifiers differ in their ability to fit arbitrary labels when the input representations stay fixed. The learned representations and the classifier's capacity make this test distinct from memorization when the whole model is trained.

  • For tested representation methods, classifier training accuracies correlate across datasets for normal and shuffled labels. Bram Wallace et al., 2020 ↗
  • Two-layer MNLI classifiers' validation accuracy varies across bag-of-words, pretrained RoBERTa-large and fine-tuned RoBERTa-large representations. Gregory Yauney et al., 2021 ↗
Continued random-data learning depends on plasticity 4 studies

Models can learn additional random data or successive random-label tasks. Their ability to keep learning and retain prior capabilities depends on plasticity—the capacity to adapt—and the training procedure.

  • Tested models fit combined original and random data nearly perfectly after their vocabulary is enlarged. Xiaotian Zhang et al., 2026 ↗
Consistent label inversion can remain learnable 2 studies

Consistently inverting binary labels can preserve a learnable task. Training loss need not increase monotonically with the label-flip rate.

  • In the HDFS dataset, fully inverted labels yield lower, decreasing training loss than partially flipped labels. Aftab Hussain et al., 2022 ↗
V2Random labels add modest training time, with convergence slowing as corruption increases 2241

Suggested status Ccontested

Several independent studies find that convergence slows as label corruption increases, but whether the added training time is small remains disputed. Some runs fail to fit the labels, and similar Llama fine-tuning loss curves do not show how much longer fitting takes when training conditions are matched.

Original resultZhang et al., 2016 ↗

Zhang et al. compared convergence times for Inception, Alexnet and MLP 1x512 on CIFAR10.

Relative convergence-time curves covered label-corruption fractions from 0 to 1. The available evidence provides no numerical time ratios.

Related findings2 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Fitting speed depends on data and optimization 28 studies

Memorization speed and convergence depend on input geometry, target complexity, capacity, initialization and optimization. Randomness alone does not determine a universal ordering of fitting difficulty.

  • Adam with sigmoid units fails to converge on flattened XOR in the tested two-unit networks. G. Swirszcz et al., 2017 ↗
  • Activation choice changes convergence speed in fixed-feature regression; Swish fails to converge within budget. Austin R. Benson et al., 2020 ↗
  • Tested transformers' random-label memorization time grows roughly exponentially with dataset information per unit of capacity. Yiding Song et al., 2026 ↗
Pretraining changes later memorization and transfer 19 studies

Prior training can improve transfer, accelerate later memorization or impair subsequent learning. Outcomes depend on the learned representation, downstream objective and treatment of the encoder.

  • Random-label cross-pretraining improves downstream validation accuracy on HMDB51 and UCF-101. Vinaychandran Pondenkandath et al., 2018 ↗
  • Random-label ResNet-20 pretraining gives iteratively magnitude-pruned subnetworks no early benefit; longer pretraining hurts accuracy. Jonathan Frankle et al., 2020 ↗
  • Noisy-pretrained GoogLeNet memorizes an incorrectly relabeled example faster than its clean-pretrained counterpart. Mahsa Forouzesh et al., 2022 ↗

V4Networks can fit corrupted labels while test performance degrades 1476013

Suggested status Ccontested

Independent image-classification studies reproduce perfect training fit alongside worsening test performance as label corruption increases. This does not hold in every setting: some training regimes prevent perfect fitting, and intermediate amounts of uniformly random label noise can leave test performance nearly unchanged.

Original resultZhang et al., 2016 ↗

Zhang et al. trained Inception, Alexnet, and MLP 1x512 on CIFAR10 with increasing random label corruption.

Zhang et al. plotted test error after convergence for corruption fractions from 0 to 1. These results give no numerical error values or corresponding training-fit measurements, so they do not establish both perfect fitting and worsening test performance.

Related findings8 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

More corruption can reduce held-out performance 37 studies

Held-out performance often declines as partial label corruption increases over the tested ranges. These results do not establish perfect training fit, strict monotonicity or a chance endpoint.

  • Cross-entropy test accuracy falls with symmetric CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 corruption; training-label fitting is unreported. Rumeng Yi et al., 2022 ↗
  • ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50's multi-label UCMerced test mean average precision falls as injected noise increases. A. Aksoy et al., 2020 ↗
  • Fashion-MNIST test accuracy with categorical cross-entropy falls as asymmetric label noise increases. B. Damodaran et al., 2019 ↗
Error structure matters at matched corruption rates 31 studies

The structure of annotation errors changes fitting and held-out performance beyond the overall error rate. Spatially concentrated errors, speech error types and structured image-label errors have different effects from random corruption.

  • Locally clustered MNIST label errors yield lower overall prediction accuracy than randomly spread errors. Amnon Drory et al., 2020 ↗
  • At matched word-level error rates, deletions harm RNN-T performance more than substitutions or insertions. I-Fan Chen et al., 2021 ↗
  • BiomedCLIP's structured errors lower PCAM test area under the curve more than equally frequent random errors. Bruce Changlong Xu et al., 2026 ↗
Similar training fit can hide different generalization 29 studies

Similar or perfect training fit can coexist with different held-out performance and representation quality. Which solution training finds matters, as do architecture, initialization and training history.

  • Synthetic two-layer ReLU CNN approaches zero training loss and optimal (Bayes) test error despite label corruption. Yi-Wen Kou et al., 2023 ↗
  • An algorithm constructed to fit every label scores lower on true CIFAR-10 labels than trained ResNet18. Li-Jia Yu et al., 2024 ↗
  • Label permutation increases PPA reconstruction distance despite nearly perfect ResNet training accuracy. Rasmus Torp et al., 2026 ↗
Generalization after interpolation depends on the solution 20 studies

Noisy interpolators can generalize under specific assumptions about the estimator, features, signal and geometry. Other settings retain substantial excess risk despite small training loss.

  • The ideal Gaussian-feature linear interpolator has an excess-MSE bound under specified dimensional conditions. Vidya K. Muthukumar et al., 2019 ↗
  • Under specified kernel-limit conditions and Gaussian noise, excess risk falls as interpolating solutions grow in norm. Zi-Tong Yang et al., 2021 ↗
  • A two-layer network on spherical inputs retains substantial excess risk despite tiny training loss. Tong-Tong Liang et al., 2026 ↗
Fitting labels does not establish perturbation robustness 8 studies

Robustness around memorized examples depends on the task and perturbation. Fitting noisy labels can coexist with fragile predictions and poor adversarial robustness.

  • Shuffled-label training error under small FGSM (fast-gradient-sign) attacks grows as a power law of attack size. E. Cubuk et al., 2017 ↗
  • Adversarial training (PGD-AT, TRADES) fails to reach near-perfect robust random-label training accuracy within the tested budget. Yin-Peng Dong et al., 2021 ↗
Test risk can peak near perfect training fit 7 studies

Test risk can rise near the point where models fit every training label, then decline with additional capacity or training. Later improvement depends on noise, features, regularization and the evaluation metric.

  • Noisy MNIST-1D test error peaks near perfect training fit, falling as MLP and CNN size increases. S. Greydanus et al., 2020 ↗
  • At tested widths and noise, error's dip before interpolation is lower than its dip after interpolation. Cory Stephenson et al., 2021 ↗
  • At fixed label corruption, test error peaks near perfect training fit, improving as parameter counts increase. Matteo Gamba et al., 2022 ↗
Simple shortcuts can harm performance on subgroups and shifted data 6 studies

Simple predictive shortcuts and example-specific nuisance features can obstruct learning of core features. Feature interventions, weighting and optimization can change subgroup and shifted-distribution performance.

  • Randomizing the simplest predictive feature collapses AUC on constructed datasets; randomizing complex features does not. Harshay Shah et al., 2020 ↗
  • Standard models struggle on examples contradicting dataset biases; the LfF method improves performance across groups. J. Nam et al., 2020 ↗
Classification success does not establish correct class probabilities 5 studies

Predicted probabilities can reflect local or corrupted label distributions. Useful classification under noise alone does not establish recovery of clean-label probabilities or calibration.

    V6Networks often learn real patterns before memorizing noisy labels 141283

    Suggested status R2independently reproduced

    Several independent groups reproduce earlier learning of clean labels followed by later noise memorization under random label corruption. This ordering can fail with structured or adversarial noise, very high corruption, and some synthetic tasks.

    Both experiments reported training and validation accuracy curves. The results are graphical, without numerical estimates of the separation between clean-label learning and noise memorization.

    Related findings7 groups of studies

    Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

    Test performance can decline after an early peak 29 studies

    Continued noisy-label training can worsen generalization after an early peak. Stopping rules and robust objectives can limit this deterioration, but test-performance curves alone do not show which examples the model fitted first.

    • Cross-entropy test accuracy improves, plateaus and then declines under partial label noise. Jason Lin et al., 2021 ↗
    • CE and SuperLoss decline late under CIFAR-100 noise, while DiscrimLoss plateaus. Tingting Wu et al., 2022 ↗
    • TLCM's and ASL's test mean average precision falls after early gains; MPVAE approaches a lower plateau. Amirmasoud Ghiassi et al., 2022 ↗
    Useful features can survive corrupted-label training 28 studies

    Useful features and previously learned information can survive noisy-label fitting or random-label retraining. Retention and accessibility depend on the layer, corruption, augmentation and probe.

    • Training to predict fixed Gaussian targets improves linear-probe accuracy over random initialization. Lang Huang et al., 2021 ↗
    • Random-label training improves true-label probes with augmentation; without it, ResNet18 training degrades CIFAR10 embeddings. Sotiris Anagnostidis et al., 2022 ↗
    • Random-label face unlearning eliminates forgotten-identity test accuracy while retaining compactness and high base retrieval. M. Zakharov, 2025 ↗
    Learning favors some functions and examples 10 studies

    Learning can favor simpler functions, lower frequencies and easier valid examples. Learning rate, initialization, input geometry and target structure affect these preferences and their generalization consequences.

      Memorization and generalization occur on different timescales 8 studies

      When a model memorizes, forgets or generalizes depends on the task, its capacity and initialization, and its kernel geometry. Useful generalization may appear briefly or emerge late.

      • In the tested modular-addition MLP, label noise delays the generalization jump after reaching a training-accuracy threshold. Havish Singavarapu, 2025 ↗
      Memorization can support rare and difficult examples 6 studies

      Information specific to rare or difficult valid examples can support generalization. Removing influential examples or correcting their labels can harm the model's learning of those examples.

      • Removing high-influence CIFAR-100 examples reduces test accuracy, mainly on the test examples they influence. V. Feldman et al., 2020 ↗
      • Self-adaptive label correction reduces minority-class accuracy relative to cross-entropy, especially under stronger imbalance. Daniel Chiu et al., 2020 ↗
      • Removing SST-2 examples that strongly influence their own predictions harms test accuracy more than random removal. Xiaosen Zheng et al., 2022 ↗
      Noisy examples affect optimization before being fitted 6 studies

      Clean and noisy examples shape gradients differently throughout training. Their relative influence depends on training time, architecture, normalization and how the model is adapted.

      • Clean-to-noisy gradient magnitudes approach parity by early stopping in binary MNIST; corruption descriptions differ. Chaoyue Liu et al., 2023 ↗
      Federated training changes fitting and generalization timing 3 studies

      Federated averaging can slow noisy-label fitting. Peak performance and test-accuracy trajectories depend on noise levels and client heterogeneity.

      • Federated models memorize noisy labels more slowly but may miss centralized training's peak test accuracy. Yu-Xin Tian et al., 2024 ↗
      • With noisy labels, federated averaging's test accuracy rises initially and then declines. Xue Jiang et al., 2022 ↗

      Settings and limits

      V5Networks can fit random labels with regularization and generalize without it 37151

      Suggested status R2independently reproduced

      Several independent groups reproduce random-label fitting with explicit regularization and useful generalization without it. This depends on the setting: regularization can suppress memorization in partially corrupted tasks.

      Original resultZhang et al., 2016 ↗

      Zhang et al. compared random-label fitting and true-label generalization with and without explicit regularizers.

      On CIFAR10, Inception reached 100% random-label training accuracy with weight decay and 99.28–99.93% with augmentation; Alexnet failed to converge with weight decay. On true labels, Inception achieved 85.75% CIFAR10 test accuracy without augmentation or weight decay, while Inception V3 achieved 59.80% ImageNet test accuracy without augmentation, dropout or weight decay.

      Related findings1 group of studies

      Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

      Regularization effects depend on the setting 30 studies

      Augmentation, weight penalties, dropout and capacity controls change fitting and generalization. Their effects depend on architecture, noise, task and optimization settings.

      • Weaker diagonal regularization raises neural tangent kernel random-label training accuracy, while test accuracy stays unchanged. A. Galloway et al., 2022 ↗
      • L2 regularization stabilizes ONN test misclassification under Gaussian target noise. Wen-Jia Wang et al., 2020 ↗
      • Selected transfer models using DRFit, ridge or Mixup have low training accuracy, with no reported overfitting. Olof Zetterqvist et al., 2021 ↗

      Diagnosing and interpreting memorization

      Use diagnostics, probes and randomized-label controls to assess corrupted supervision, retained information and the limits of aggregate performance measures.

      Corruption changes internal geometry and spectra 56 studies

      Label corruption changes the geometry of learned representations, activation statistics, and gradient or weight spectra (how strongly different directions contribute). How these measures relate to memorization and generalization depends on architecture, layer and training stage.

      • In synthetic networks, label corruption raises effective curvature, weighted parameter size and a proposed generalization-error bound. Xinyan Li et al., 2019 ↗
      • Grokking modular-division transformers have lower minimum local dimensionality than models with persistently low validation accuracy. B. Brown et al., 2022 ↗
      • Corruption raises peak Fisher effective rank, a dimensionality measure; clean and corrupted examples contribute oppositely. Satwik Bathula et al., 2026 ↗
      Detecting label errors depends on training conditions 40 studies

      Loss, curvature, influence and other diagnostic measures can identify errors in supervision. Their reliability depends on the corruption, example difficulty, learned representation and training stage.

      • Influential Rank, an influence-based method, detects corrupted CIFAR-10 labels using clean validation examples. Seulki Park et al., 2021 ↗
      • Loss curvature with respect to inputs, averaged across epochs, detects synthetic label errors with weight decay. Isha Garg et al., 2023 ↗
      • In federated learning, loss against labels detects persistent label flips better than each client's uncertainty. Bradley Scott et al., 2026 ↗
      Diagnostics reveal more than training accuracy 26 studies

      Confidence, margins, stability, agreement and complexity measures provide information about generalization beyond training fit. Their reliability depends on the model, metric and evaluation conditions.

      • L2NNNs have smaller training and test confidence gaps with random labels than clean labels. Haifeng Qian et al., 2018 ↗
      • Semantic-versus-random-label EMC advantage correlates negatively with generalization gap in CNNs and MLPs. Ravid Shwartz-Ziv et al., 2024 ↗
      • Random-label training increases joint-bank feasibility, which correlates weakly with held-out random-label accuracy. Michael Timothy Bennett, 2026 ↗
      Random labels expose evaluation leakage 8 studies

      Randomized-label controls can reveal inflated performance caused by overlapping data or model selection, while some reported validation protocols score near chance.

      • With randomized subject labels, MRI-slice accuracy stays high when training and evaluation include the same subjects. Ekin Yağış et al., 2021 ↗
      • With scrambled training labels, DAPPER's validation Matthews correlation coefficient, a classification score, stays near zero. A. Bizzego et al., 2018 ↗
      • Nested-CV and untouched external estimates remain near chance under random labels; comparison estimates are higher. Ahmad Hassanat et al., 2026 ↗
      Aggregate performance can miss retained training information 7 studies

      Attacks and probes of individual examples can reveal retained training information that overall accuracy or train–test performance gaps miss. These findings depend on the model, data and assumptions about how the attack works.

      • An attack recovers singleton bits from an MLP despite almost complete fresh-singleton classification failure. Gavin Brown et al., 2020 ↗
      • MNIST VAE memorization scores rise before train-test gaps appear; lower learning rates reduce peak scores. Gerrit J. J. van den Burg et al., 2021 ↗
      • Malicious selective aggregation increases membership-inference attack success, measured by AUC, on MNIST, EUROSAT and PATHMNIST. Soumia Zohra El Mestari et al., 2025 ↗
      Random-label training changes agreement between models on unseen inputs 6 studies

      Random-label training can change representations and agreement between predictions from separately trained models. Models that agree on fitted training labels need not make similar predictions on unseen inputs.

      • Random-label models' test-prediction agreement clusters at low and high levels, while test accuracy stays at chance. Guy Hacohen et al., 2019 ↗
      Random labels change information and compression measurements 5 studies

      Label randomization changes estimated weight information and compressibility. The interpretation depends on how information is defined and measured.

      • Small AlexNet's estimated weight information rises with label corruption under the study's penalty on weight information. Alessandro Achille et al., 2017 ↗

      Managing noisy supervision

      In the settings studied, changes to supervision, training, specialized model components and later model edits can alter how well networks fit noisy labels and learn useful patterns.

      Better supervision improves performance under label noise 85 studies

      Selecting examples, correcting labels and changing supervision can improve held-out performance under partial corruption. These gains alone do not establish reduced memorization of corrupted labels.

      • Co-teaching improves clean-test accuracy over standard CNN training with feature-correlated errors in Te data. C. Groschner et al., 2022 ↗
      • BL+FN, a noisy-label method, improves MNIST clean-test accuracy under heavy corruption; noisy-label fitting is unreported. Lu Zeng et al., 2023 ↗
      • WARw2v beats categorical cross-entropy on Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 under asymmetric label noise. B. Damodaran et al., 2019 ↗
      Training changes can reduce corrupted-label fitting 33 studies

      Modified objectives, gradient aggregation, example weighting and forgetting procedures can suppress or reverse corrupted-label fitting. Useful learning can persist under these interventions in the reported settings.

      • SIGUA forgets flipped MNIST labels and improves test accuracy when told exactly which examples are corrupted. Bo Han et al., 2018 ↗
      • Modified AllConv (IOC-AllConv) fits fully corrupted labels poorly, outperforming standard AllConv under partial corruption. S. Sivaprasad et al., 2020 ↗
      • RMD's training fit and test accuracy vary with lambda under partial CIFAR-10 corruption. Navid Azizan et al., 2022 ↗
      Dedicated components can separate memorization from useful learning 7 studies

      Dedicated heads, experts, neurons and adapters can route learning from clean labels and memorization of noisy labels into separate components. Changing these components can change model outputs while internal representations persist.

      • Example-tied dropout ResNet-9 nearly perfectly fits clean and noisy CIFAR-10 subsets before designated neurons are removed. Pratyush Maini et al., 2023 ↗
      • The tested model reaches near-zero training loss on both real and randomly assigned answers. John Li et al., 2024 ↗
      Teacher choices and training objectives affect distillation outcomes 7 studies

      Teacher selection, temperature, training objective and additional data affect distillation under noisy labels. Teacher outputs can transfer memorized information as well as task patterns that generalize.

      • Combining teachers trained on noisy labels improves test accuracy; distilling with CIFAR-5m data improves it further. Gal Kaplun et al., 2022 ↗
      • Small-temperature KL distillation generalizes best under CIFAR-100 noise; MSE does not prevent degradation above 50%. Taehyeon Kim et al., 2021 ↗
      Later interventions change memorization and held-out performance 3 studies

      Classifier editing, feature projection and targeted continuation can alter memorized information and held-out performance. Outcomes depend on the layer, evaluation data and intervention strength.

        Other forms of memorization

        This section covers memorization in generative models, learning from images and text, and remembering details of inputs, beyond fitting labels in classifiers.

        Generative models retain training structure in different ways 3 studies

        Autoencoder attraction and diffusion score interpolation can retain training-specific structure. Population behavior depends on architecture, initialization, sample size, smoothing and stopping.

        • An MNIST autoencoder reconstructs well; repeatedly feeding test-image reconstructions back as inputs converges to training examples. Adityanarayanan Radhakrishnan et al., 2018 ↗
        Mismatched image-text pairs change alignment and memorization 3 studies

        Noisy image-text correspondences change alignment and measured memorization. The training procedure affects how well clean and mismatched pairs separate.

        • Mis-captioned COCO pairs have higher memorization scores than clean pairs; clean-pair scores stay similar across models. Wen-Hao Wang et al., 2025 ↗
        • During training, method SDD increasingly separates clean and mismatched Flickr30K pairs; method NPC's early separation weakens. Fan Liu et al., 2024 ↗
        Memorization can retain irrelevant input details 2 studies

        Networks can retain unique or task-irrelevant input features. Architecture, augmentation, training randomness and feature alignment affect this retention, which different memorization measures may capture differently.

        • Augmentation increases measured unique-feature memorization in a CIFAR-10 CNN; this measure does not assess random-label fitting. J. Hartley et al., 2022 ↗

        1. 1

          Chiyuan Zhang et al., 2016 ↗ Understanding deep learning requires rethinking generalization

          Establishes the baseline random-label experiments, including training fit, test performance, corruption sweeps and regularizer removal.

        2. 2

          Devansh Arpit et al., 2017 ↗ A Closer Look at Memorization in Deep Networks

          Examines learning order under partial corruption and how tuned dropout reduces random-label fitting while preserving clean-data learning.

        3. 3

          Koby Bibas et al., 2019 ↗ Deep pNML: Predictive Normalized Maximum Likelihood for Deep Neural Networks

          Pairs perfect training fit with declining test accuracy across corruption rates, including fully random labels.

        Known gaps in this draft

        The main gaps concern matched training conditions, measured fitting times, evidence at larger scales, learning order, source reliability and independent reproduction.

        All 7 gaps
        • Complete random-label fitting under unchanged hyperparameters and training budgets remains unresolved across settings. Some successful fits required longer training, a different learning rate or removal of regularization and augmentation.
        • How much random labels slow training remains poorly established. Similar loss curves and qualitative reports of slower learning do not establish that fitting takes only a small multiple of the usual training time.
        • At billion-parameter scale, some results have not been independently reproduced. Qwen3-14B's nearly complete fitting does not establish that every training example was fitted, and its reported fitting on TinyImageNet-200 remains incomplete.
        • Learning clean examples before corrupted examples is not established across asymmetric, feature-dependent, adversarial and very high noise. Declining held-out performance alone cannot establish the order in which examples are fitted.
        • Disagreements about augmentation, noise sensitivity and worsening test performance need comparisons with matched training procedures and budgets. An ImageNet run stopped before fitting all training examples, leaving it unknown whether fitting would eventually finish.
        • Some influential reports of failed or reversed effects remain qualitative or lack final numerical results and uncertainty estimates. For other findings, discrepancies between the reported results and the cited passages remain unresolved.
        • It is unclear whether some apparently corroborating reports are independent: they include the same publications under different names, overlapping studies and shared authors. These relationships need clarification before judging how broadly findings have been reproduced.
